name: agent-eval-bench
oneLiner: An evaluation bench that scores a tool-using agent's **execution trace**, not the text of its answer.
summary: The contract came before the code: `docs/SPEC.md` is 55 kB of specification with sixteen behaviours and seven hard constraints, each citing the scenarios that prove it. Thirty-five scenarios sit as YAML data validated by a strict JSON Schema, in five classes: happy, ambiguity, denied, adversarial, degradation. Layer 1 is twelve deterministic assertion types over the captured trace — no model, no network, no credentials — so it can block every pull request. Layer 2 is an LLM judge with anchored rubrics, a pinned model and the prompt hash in the report. The demonstration is an HR agent filing a leave request that stops short of the write: the approval gate is enforced by a **single-use token from a CSPRNG**, not by an instruction in the prompt — you can talk the agent into writing, but not into producing a token that was never issued. A scenario runs through the service's real composition root; failures are injected at the tool seam, so a degradation scenario takes the same code path as a real timeout.
tests: 235 [Fact]/[Theory] attributes in the sources (221 Fact, 14 Theory) plus 10 Playwright tests; 35 scenarios / 313 assertions, baseline 35/35 pass
ci: Nine workflows. `ci.yml` has seven jobs — lint-docs, lint-actions, lint-shell, architecture, coupling, build-test, e2e (counted from the `jobs:` keys after parsing the file) — including a coupling check: changing the prompt requires changing the specification, changing a rubric requires a version bump. On top of that, a nightly judged run and a production loop scoring real spans.

docs.label: The whole thing in one document

components.name: AssertionEvaluator — warstwa 1
components.description: Twelve deterministic assertion types over the trace. None of them passes vacuously, and an unknown type is an error, not a pass.

components.name: ConfirmationTokenStore
components.description: A write gate enforced by a 256-bit token from a CSPRNG, issued when the draft is shown and redeemed exactly once. The pattern is domain-independent — the dependency on the draft is four fields.

components.name: Walidatory repozytorium
components.description: Node scripts in CI: scenario validation, link checking, diagram parity, EN/PL document parity, change-coupling checking.

components.name: Schemat scenariusza (JSON Schema)
components.description: A strict contract for the scenario file: classes, fixture delta, permitted assertion types. It is not portable between domains: `$defs/toolName` is a closed enum of five HR tools (`get_current_user`, `find_employee`, `list_leave_types`, `list_leaves`, `request_time_off`) mirroring the `IWorkforceTools` interface and referenced from seven places in the schema (`fixture.tool_behaviour` plus `tool`/`source_tool` in assertions); `$defs/eventName` is closed the same way. The format itself is independent of .NET, but another domain has to edit both enums.

components.name: RubricJudge i kalibracja
components.description: A judge with rubrics anchored per level, a pinned model, a prompt hash and {{term:kappa|Cohen's kappa}} arithmetic. Without credentials it reports `skipped`, never a quiet green.

components.name: BrokenAgents — pass mutacyjny
components.description: Four deliberately broken agent variants and a scenario that has to catch each one. On the first run the variant that writes twice passed two scenarios — and that was fixed in the scenarios, not in the variant.

components.name: AgentOrchestrator (11 steps)
components.description: The order of the steps **is** the specification: EstablishActor → … → ConfirmationGate → ExecuteWrite, with exactly one recorded outcome and one termination reason.

overlaps.reason: This is the reference implementation of the AI-EVALS standard from that repository; `DEVIATIONS.md` is a line-by-line reckoning, and the corrections go back into the standard.
Also does an LLM judge over an agent trace, with calibration and mutation testing — only as an asynchronous worker on a queue instead of a harness in CI.
Has the {{term:playhead|record/replay cassette}} this repository lacks — and without it layer 2 cannot tell a regression from model randomness.
The private recruitment repository accompanying this project, with the same case as its integration target.

product: The buyer is real, but it is not the team building the agent — it is whoever has to **prove** that the agent does not do the things it must not. This is an {{term:evidence|audit export}}, not another dashboard. The repository itself is the best credibility artefact in the portfolio today: contract before code, absence assertions, a mutation pass and an explicit register of deviations are a set almost nobody shows publicly.
highlights: Nineteen per cent of the assertions are **absence assertions** — checking what the agent did not do. That is the rarest and hardest part of evaluating agents, and here it is enforced by the schema: a `denied` or `adversarial` scenario without an absence assertion is rejected in CI.

The approval gate is enforced in three independent places: a single-use token in the code, the agent's declaration in `definition.json` and an assertion in the scenario. The prompt is the fourth and the weakest.
The suite caught fourteen defects, **seven of them in the instrument itself or in the specification** — that is, the measuring tool was tested against itself.
Without credentials the judge reports `skipped:no-credential`. Never green. That is a one-line design decision that separates a harness from theatre.
CI watches the coupling between documents: you cannot change the prompt without changing the specification, nor a rubric without a version bump.
gaps: No {{term:determinizm|replay layer}}. Without one, layer 2 cannot tell a regression from model randomness — and that is exactly the gap kernel K1 closes, and this is its first consumer.

Layer 2 has never run against a live model, the MCP adapter has never spoken to a real server, the deployment to Fly never happened. All three are honestly written up as deviations — but they are still promises, not facts.
Twenty-one open issues against one pull request — that is a backlog, not activity.
The judge calibration has forty-five labels from **one** rater, and that rater is an AI. {{term:kappa|Kappa}} with a single rater measures consistency, not agreement with a human.
next: Wire in the {{term:playhead|cassette}} from K1 and switch layer 2 to replay mode. That is one dependency and one configuration change, and it unblocks CI for the judging layer.
Run layer 2 once against a live model, record the run, and replay it from then on. One cost instead of a continuing one.
Add a second, human rater for the calibration — without one the kappa figure is technically correct and empty.
Close or tidy the twenty-one issues; a public repo with that ratio of issues to PRs looks abandoned.
risks: The address `agent-eval-bench-demo.fly.dev` is declared in the configuration and there is nothing behind it. A deployment address that does not answer is worse than no address at all.
headline: First consumer of kernel K1 — without replay, regression looks like randomness
